quizzes.title: Orbits: LEO, MEO and GEO
quizzes.passage:
An orbit is the curved path that a satellite follows around Earth under the influence of gravity. Mission designers must weigh several trade-offs before they choose one, and no single orbit suits every purpose. Earth orbits are classified by altitude, by inclination and by shape. Shape refers to whether an orbit is circular or elliptical, and inclination refers to its tilt relative to the Equator.

Satellites are commonly grouped into three broad families. The first family is Low Earth Orbit, the closest of the three to the planet. Its satellites are widely used for Earth observation and communication, and crewed platforms such as the International Space Station also operate in this zone. Several sub-types exist for particular purposes, including the Sun-synchronous orbit and the Very Low Earth Orbit. Both of these are sub-types of Low Earth Orbit.

The second family is Medium Earth Orbit. Mission planners place it beyond the first family but below the third. The third family is Geosynchronous Orbit, and Geostationary Orbit is a special case within it. Geostationary Orbit is used for communication, weather and imaging. Each family is described in order of increasing distance from Earth, and each differs in altitude, latency and typical use.

questions.q: Approximately how long does one orbit take for a satellite in Low Earth Orbit?
questions.explanation: The booklet gives the orbital period of Low Earth Orbit as around 90 to 120 minutes.

questions.q: Which orbit family is described as providing a balance between coverage area and signal latency?
questions.explanation: The booklet says Medium Earth Orbit provides a balance between coverage area and signal latency.

questions.q: What apparent ground movement may a geosynchronous satellite that is not geostationary show?
options: It appears stationary over one point
It may appear to move North-South
questions.explanation: The booklet notes that a geosynchronous satellite may appear to move North-South, unlike a geostationary one.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A geostationary satellite appears fixed over one particular point on Earth.
Reason (R): Its orbit lies directly over the Equator with zero-degree inclination and it moves in the same direction as Earth's rotation.
Select the correct option.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: The booklet ties the fixed appearance of a geostationary satellite to its zero-degree orbit over the Equator, moving with Earth's rotation.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Low Earth Orbit
II. Medium Earth Orbit
III. Very Low Earth Orbit
IV. Geostationary Orbit
A. Global navigation satellite systems
B. Altitude of about 35,786 km
C. Altitude of about 160 to 2,000 km
D. Greater atmospheric drag
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.explanation: Low Earth Orbit matches C, Medium Earth Orbit matches A, Very Low Earth Orbit matches D and Geostationary Orbit matches B.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about orbits:
I. Low Earth Orbit satellites are suited to large satellite constellations.
II. Medium Earth Orbit is primarily used by weather satellites.
III. Low Earth Orbit offers low communication latency.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is wrong because the booklet names navigation as the main use of Medium Earth Orbit, while I and III are stated for Low Earth Orbit.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about geosynchronous and geostationary satellites are correct?
I. A geosynchronous satellite's orbital period equals Earth's rotational period.
II. Medium Earth Orbit lies below the altitude range of Low Earth Orbit.
III. A geostationary satellite may be inclined to the Equator.
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since Medium Earth Orbit lies above Low Earth Orbit and a geostationary satellite has zero-degree inclination.

quizzes.title: Reading Satellite Orbits
quizzes.passage:
An orbit is the curved path a satellite follows around Earth under the influence of gravity. Different orbits suit different missions, and the orbit a satellite uses determines the kind of work it can do. Earth orbits are classified by altitude, by inclination and by shape. Inclination is the tilt of an orbit relative to the Equator, and shape refers to whether an orbit is circular or elliptical. Some families lie close to the planet, while others lie far above it. Navigation systems also rely on satellites placed in one of these families.

The lowest family is often used for Earth observation and communication, and it suits large constellations of satellites. Low communication latency is a key feature of this family. Crewed space stations also operate in this closer region. Within the lowest family, specialised sub-types exist for particular purposes. Each family is linked to particular mission applications.

A middle family lies farther away than the lowest family. The highest family, known as geosynchronous, is defined by the timing of a satellite's revolution relative to the planet's spin. A special member of this family appears to hang above one place on the ground, which makes it useful for watching the same region continuously.

questions.q: What is the approximate upper altitude limit, in km, of Low Earth Orbit?
questions.explanation: The booklet gives Low Earth Orbit as approximately 160 to 2,000 km above Earth.

questions.q: What is the lower end, in minutes, of the orbital period range given for Low Earth Orbit?
questions.explanation: The booklet gives the orbital period of Low Earth Orbit as around 90 to 120 minutes.

questions.q: Name the European navigation system that the booklet cites as an example of a Medium Earth Orbit system (one word).
questions.explanation: The booklet names GPS and Europe's Galileo as examples of Medium Earth Orbit navigation systems.

questions.q: Which Low Earth Orbit sub-type enables very high-resolution observations but experiences greater atmospheric drag? (name the sub-type)
questions.explanation: The booklet says Very Low Earth Orbit enables very high-resolution observations but experiences greater atmospheric drag.

questions.q: What is the approximate altitude, in km, of Geosynchronous Orbit?
questions.explanation: The booklet places Geosynchronous Orbit at approximately 35,786 km above Earth.

questions.q: A geosynchronous orbit's period equals 23 hours, 56 minutes and how many seconds? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet gives Earth's rotational period as 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds.

questions.q: Which orbit family does the booklet describe as offering wider coverage with moderate latency? (acronym)
questions.explanation: The booklet's orbit table lists Medium Earth Orbit as offering wider coverage with moderate latency.

quizzes.title: EOS-05 Imaging Uses
quizzes.passage:
ISRO launched Earth Observation Satellite 05, known as EOS-05, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota. The satellite is also called GISAT-1A, and the booklet describes it as India's first dedicated imaging satellite. It is designed to operate from a sub-geosynchronous orbit.

The launch validated India's cryogenic upper-stage technology for future human spaceflight, according to the booklet. The booklet also says it is the heaviest payload a GSLV has injected into orbit. Its launch was the nineteenth operational flight of the GSLV.

A low orbit satellite sees a given location only when it passes overhead, which leaves gaps between observations. A satellite that stays over one region of the planet can instead keep a wide area under watch for long periods. The booklet lists a fixed, 24/7 footprint over the Indian subcontinent as a geostationary advantage. Such platforms are described as useful for tracking cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires.

EOS-05 is equipped with optical and infrared imaging payloads, and its applications are presented under three headings: disaster management, strategic and national security, and agriculture and environment. Each heading is linked to a set of monitoring tasks, and the booklet lists examples under each one. The booklet presents these points together in a short summary of the satellite and its applications.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the application areas that the booklet gives for EOS-05?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists disaster management, strategic and national security, and agriculture and environment as the three application areas.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a purpose that frequent observations can support?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists weather monitoring, disaster management, early warning and emergency response, but not mineral exploration.

questions.q: How does the booklet describe cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires?
questions.explanation: The booklet refers to cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires as rapidly developing events.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Crop insurance claims can be settled using objective satellite indices.
Reason (R): Satellite indices replace manual experiments in the claim process.
Select the correct option.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: The booklet says crop insurance claims are streamlined because manual experiments are replaced by objective satellite indices.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Optical sensors
II. High altitude
III. Strategic and national security
IV. Agriculture and environment
A. Monitoring of forest fires, vegetation health and crop cycles
B. Continuous surveillance of land borders and maritime domain
C. Cannot penetrate thick clouds
D. Limits sub-meter spatial resolution
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.explanation: Optical sensors match C, high altitude matches D, strategic and national security matches B and agriculture and environment matches A.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about EOS-05 applications:
I. Frequent observations can support early warning and emergency response.
II. Strategic security applications include enhancing situational awareness.
III. Disaster management applications include tracking the maritime domain.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement III is wrong because the maritime domain is listed under strategic security, while I and II are stated in the booklet.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about EOS-05 are correct?
I. EOS-05 enables gapless cyclone tracking.
II. Crop insurance claims rely on manual field experiments rather than satellite indices.
III. Forest fire monitoring is part of the strategic and national security application area.
questions.explanation: Only statement I is correct, since crop insurance claims use satellite indices and forest fire monitoring belongs to agriculture and environment.

quizzes.title: Why Geostationary Imaging Helps
quizzes.passage:
A satellite in a low orbit sees a given location only when it passes overhead, which leaves gaps between observations. A satellite that stays over one region of the planet can instead keep a wide area under watch for long periods.

The booklet connects this kind of monitoring with several tasks. Persistent watch can help track storms and floods, and it can support warnings issued before a hazard grows. Surveillance of the sea approaches and the land frontiers is also mentioned, as are checks on plant cover and forest condition. The booklet also says that the use of such data can streamline crop insurance claims.

EOS-05 is India's first dedicated imaging satellite and is also known by another name. It carries optical and infrared imaging payloads, and it is designed to operate from a sub-geosynchronous orbit. The satellite's optical sensors form one part of its imaging system, and the booklet also notes that the sensors face physical limits.

Another listed advantage is a steady footprint that stays fixed over the same land all day. Cyclones, cloudbursts and flash floods are among the events that the booklet mentions. The booklet presents these uses as part of the satellite's significance for India. Each use is described with a short list of examples.

questions.q: Name the application area of EOS-05 that the booklet links with continuous surveillance of land borders and the maritime domain.
questions.explanation: The booklet places continuous surveillance of land borders and the maritime domain under strategic and national security.

questions.q: Name the application area that the booklet links with monitoring of forest fires, vegetation health and crop cycles.
questions.explanation: The booklet lists forest fires, vegetation health and crop cycles under agriculture and environment.

questions.q: By what other name is EOS-05 known, according to the booklet?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that EOS-05 is also called GISAT-1A.

questions.q: Over which region does the booklet say a geostationary advantage gives a fixed, 24/7 footprint? (name the region)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the geostationary advantage maintains a fixed, 24/7 footprint over the Indian subcontinent.

questions.q: Through what weather feature are optical sensors unable to see? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that optical sensors cannot penetrate thick clouds.

questions.q: What kind of data replaces manual experiments in crop insurance claims? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says crop insurance claims are streamlined by replacing manual experiments with objective satellite indices.

questions.q: What phrase does the booklet use to describe cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet refers to these hazards as rapidly developing events.
